cards.back: Burning plastics, wool, silk, and synthetic furnishings in structure fires. Rapid loss of consciousness, seizures, and cardiovascular collapse with normal-looking skin. Hydroxocobalamin is the antidote, carried by ALS.

cards.front: What do SLUDGEM and DUMBELS stand for, and which findings kill?
cards.back: SLUDGEM: salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, gastric upset, emesis, miosis. DUMBELS adds bradycardia, bronchorrhea, and bronchospasm, and those three Bs are what kill. Antidotes are atropine and pralidoxime.

cards.front: How does heat exhaustion differ from heat stroke?
cards.back: Heat exhaustion has heavy sweating, pale cool clammy skin, and intact mental status. Heat stroke is a core temperature over 104 F with altered mental status and hot skin, which may be dry or soaked.

cards.front: How do you cool a heat stroke patient?
cards.back: Cold-water or ice-water immersion is fastest for exertional heat stroke. Otherwise strip the patient, wet the skin, fan aggressively, and pack ice at the neck, armpits, and groin. Keep cooling en route. No antipyretics.

cards.front: Give the three hypothermia stages with core temperatures.
cards.back: Mild 90 to 95 F: shivering, alert, clumsy. Moderate 82 to 90 F: shivering stops, confusion, bradycardia. Severe below 82 F: unresponsive, rigid, undetectable pulse, high ventricular fibrillation risk.

cards.front: Why do you rewarm the trunk rather than the arms and legs?
cards.back: Warming the extremities first dilates them and sends cold acidic blood back to the core, called afterdrop, which can drop the core temperature further and trigger arrhythmias.

cards.front: How long do you check for a pulse in a severely hypothermic patient, and what is the saying?
cards.back: A full 30 to 60 seconds, because the rate can be extremely slow and faint. The saying is not dead until warm and dead: resuscitation continues until the patient is rewarmed at the hospital.

cards.front: Why is drowning managed differently from an adult cardiac arrest?
cards.back: The cause is hypoxia, not a rhythm problem, so ventilation comes early, in the water when safe. Skip abdominal thrusts for water, expect vomiting, and restrict spinal motion only if the mechanism suggests injury.

cards.front: Why does lightning use reverse triage?
cards.back: Lightning causes cardiac and respiratory arrest that often responds to prompt resuscitation, while those still moving will generally survive without you. So with multiple victims you treat the pulseless and apneic first.

cards.front: What do you do and not do for a snakebite?
cards.back: Keep the patient calm, remove rings and watches, immobilize the limb at or below heart level, mark the leading edge of swelling with a time, and transport. No tourniquet, no ice, no cutting, no suction.

cards.front: What medical causes must you rule out before calling behavior psychiatric?
cards.back: Hypoglycemia, hypoxia, head injury, drugs and alcohol, stroke, and infection, especially urinary infection in an older adult. Check a glucose and a saturation on every behavioral call.

cards.front: What are the rules for physical restraint?
cards.back: Last resort, per protocol with law enforcement and medical direction. Never prone, because of positional asphyxia. One person per limb, supine or side-lying, continuous airway monitoring, distal circulation checks every 5 to 10 minutes, and full documentation.

cards.front: Should you ask a patient directly about suicide?
cards.back: Yes. Ask plainly whether they are thinking about killing themselves and whether they have a plan. Asking does not plant the idea and is the only way to find out. The national line is 988.

cards.front: What warns you that an agitated patient is about to arrest?
cards.back: Excited or hyperactive delirium: extreme agitation, apparent insensitivity to pain, unusual strength, and hyperthermia. A sudden calm after a violent struggle is a pre-arrest sign, not cooperation.

cards.front: What are the BLS sepsis alert criteria?
cards.back: Suspected infection plus two or more of: temperature above 38 C or below 36 C, heart rate above 90, respiratory rate above 20, altered mental status, or systolic under 90 or 40 below baseline.

cards.front: What are the rules around a dialysis fistula arm?
cards.back: No blood pressure, no IV, and no blood draw in that arm, ever. You can feel a buzzing thrill over the access. Damaging it costs the patient their dialysis lifeline.

cards.front: What triggers a sickle cell crisis and what is the deadliest complication?
cards.back: Dehydration, cold, infection, low oxygen, and hard exertion make cells sickle and jam small vessels. Acute chest syndrome, with chest pain, fever, cough, and hypoxia, is a leading cause of death.

quiz.q: What is the standard EMT nebulizer dose of albuterol for an adult with bronchospasm?
choices: 2.5 mg in 3 mL of saline
0.3 mg in 3 mL of saline
5 mg in 1 mL of saline
10 mg in 5 mL of saline
quiz.why: The unit dose is 2.5 mg in 3 mL of normal saline, run at 6 to 8 lpm of oxygen for about 10 minutes. 0.3 mg is the epinephrine auto-injector dose, and the other two are not standard albuterol packaging.

quiz.q: A 62-year-old with congestive heart failure is sitting bolt upright, anxious, with crackles throughout both lungs, SpO2 84 percent, and blood pressure 168/94. He is alert and following commands. Which intervention is most appropriate?
choices: Albuterol by nebulizer
CPAP at 5 to 10 cm H2O with high-flow oxygen
Lay him flat and assist ventilations
Nasal cannula at 4 lpm and rapid transport
quiz.why: CPAP pushes fluid out of the alveoli and back into circulation, and he meets every requirement: awake, cooperative, breathing on his own, and not hypotensive. Albuterol treats bronchospasm rather than fluid, and laying a pulmonary edema patient flat drowns him faster.

quiz.q: Which finding most strongly separates pneumonia from an asthma exacerbation?
choices: Shortness of breath at rest
Tachycardia
Fever with crackles localized to one area of the chest
A history of smoking
quiz.why: Pneumonia is an infection filling alveoli in one region, so it produces fever with focal crackles, while asthma produces diffuse expiratory wheezing without fever. Dyspnea, tachycardia, and a smoking history occur in both and separate nothing.

quiz.q: An asthmatic has been working hard to breathe for 40 minutes. He is now drowsy, his respiratory rate has fallen from 34 to 10, and his wheezing has quieted. What is happening?
choices: He is responding to the albuterol
His anxiety has resolved and his airways have relaxed
He is developing a pneumothorax
He is tiring into respiratory failure and needs assisted ventilation now
quiz.why: A falling rate with rising drowsiness after prolonged work of breathing is exhaustion and carbon dioxide retention, and the quiet chest means air is barely moving. Improvement would show a comfortable patient with a normal rate, not a sleepy one with a rate of 10.

quiz.q: What is the correct pediatric epinephrine auto-injector dose for a child weighing about 20 kg?
choices: 0.3 mg intramuscularly
0.15 mg intramuscularly
0.05 mg intramuscularly
1 mg intramuscularly
quiz.why: The junior auto-injector delivers 0.15 mg for a child under about 30 kg. 0.3 mg is the adult dose, 1 mg is the intravenous cardiac arrest dose, and 0.05 mg is not a manufactured auto-injector strength.

quiz.q: A man stung by a wasp 8 minutes ago has hives, wheezing, and a blood pressure of 78/40. You give epinephrine. Ten minutes later he is still wheezing with a systolic of 82. What is the next step?
choices: Give diphenhydramine and continue transport
Give a second nebulizer treatment and wait
Give a second dose of epinephrine 0.3 mg IM
Withhold further epinephrine because of the risk of tachycardia
quiz.why: Epinephrine can be repeated at 5 to 15 minutes when symptoms persist, and many anaphylaxis patients need more than one dose. An antihistamine does not reverse shock or bronchospasm, and tachycardia is an expected effect, not a reason to let a patient stay hypotensive.

quiz.q: Which patient meets the definition of anaphylaxis rather than a simple allergic reaction?
choices: A woman with hives on both arms after a new detergent, no other symptoms
A man with a swollen, red, itchy sting site on his forearm
A child with a runny nose and watery eyes during pollen season
A man with hives and abdominal cramping with vomiting 10 minutes after eating peanuts
quiz.why: Skin plus gastrointestinal involvement is two body systems after a likely allergen, which meets the definition even with a normal blood pressure. The other three describe single-system reactions with no respiratory or cardiovascular compromise.

quiz.q: Why is the anterolateral thigh the preferred site for intramuscular epinephrine?
choices: The large, well-perfused vastus lateralis gives the fastest peak blood level
It is the only site with no risk of hitting a nerve
The thigh absorbs drugs more slowly, prolonging the effect
It is the only site where the auto-injector needle is long enough
quiz.why: Peak levels occur in about 8 minutes from the thigh, faster than the deltoid or any subcutaneous route, because of muscle mass and blood supply. Slower absorption would be a disadvantage, and needle length is not the limiting factor.

quiz.q: Which three findings make up the Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale?
choices: Balance, eyes, and grip strength
Pupil size, gag reflex, and speech
Facial droop, arm drift, and abnormal speech
Level of consciousness, blood pressure, and glucose
quiz.why: The Cincinnati scale is facial droop, arm drift, and abnormal speech, and any one abnormal item gives about a 72 percent probability of stroke. Balance and eyes belong to the broader BE-FAST screen, and the other options are not part of any stroke scale.

quiz.q: A 74-year-old has left-sided weakness and slurred speech that began 90 minutes ago. The nearest hospital is 6 minutes away and is not a stroke center. A primary stroke center is 16 minutes away and a comprehensive center is 27 minutes away. Glucose is 104. What is the best destination?
choices: The nearest hospital, because time matters most
The comprehensive stroke center regardless of transport time
Whichever facility the family prefers
A stroke center, choosing per regional protocol, with an early stroke alert
quiz.why: He is inside the 4.5-hour thrombolytic window, so he needs a facility that can actually treat him, and regional protocol defines which center. The nearest hospital would have to transfer him out, and blanket routing to a comprehensive center regardless of time is not how destination rules are written.

quiz.q: What does last known well mean in a stroke assessment?
choices: The last time the patient was observed to be at their normal baseline
The time the patient was found with symptoms
The time EMS arrived on scene
The time the symptoms were first reported to dispatch
quiz.why: The treatment clock starts from the last moment anyone saw the patient normal, which may be many hours before discovery. Using the discovery or dispatch time can wrongly place a patient inside a treatment window they are not eligible for.

quiz.q: A patient with sudden right-sided weakness has a glucose of 38 mg/dL and is able to swallow. What should you do?
choices: Transport as a stroke alert without treatment
Give oral glucose 15 g and recheck in 15 minutes
Give nothing by mouth because stroke patients aspirate
Give oxygen by non-rebreather and reassess in 10 minutes
quiz.why: At 38 mg/dL the weakness is far more likely to be a hypoglycemic mimic, and it reverses in minutes with sugar. Withholding glucose to protect a possible stroke pathway leaves a fixable cause untreated, and oxygen does nothing for a fuel problem.

quiz.q: Which action is appropriate during an active generalized tonic-clonic seizure?
choices: Insert an oral airway to protect the tongue
Hold the arms and legs still to prevent injury
Place a bite block between the teeth
Move objects away, pad the head, and time the seizure
quiz.why: You protect the patient from the environment without restraining them and you time the event, because duration drives the decision about status epilepticus. Anything placed in the mouth breaks teeth and gets aspirated, and restraint causes fractures and dislocations.

quiz.q: A 30-year-old had a witnessed seizure lasting 90 seconds and is now sleepy, confused, and hard to rouse 5 minutes later. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Normal postictal state
A second seizure is imminent
Head injury from the fall
Opioid overdose
quiz.why: Postictal confusion and sleepiness lasting minutes to an hour is the expected recovery from a generalized seizure. Head injury deserves a look but is not the most likely cause without trauma findings, and opioid overdose would show pinpoint pupils and slow breathing.

quiz.q: A 30-year-old woman who is 32 weeks pregnant has a seizure at home. What is the most appropriate positioning and concern?
choices: Supine and flat, with concern for hypoglycemia
Left lateral position, with concern for eclampsia
Sitting upright, with concern for a first-time epilepsy diagnosis
Prone, with concern for aspiration
quiz.why: A seizure past 20 weeks is eclampsia until proven otherwise, and the left lateral position both protects the airway and keeps the uterus off the vena cava. Prone positioning risks asphyxia, and supine after 20 weeks reduces venous return.

quiz.q: A 70-year-old describes the sudden onset of the worst headache of his life, peaking within seconds, with vomiting and neck stiffness. What is the concern?
choices: Tension headache from stress
Migraine with aura
Subarachnoid hemorrhage
Sinus infection
quiz.why: A thunderclap headache reaching maximum intensity in seconds, especially with meningeal signs, is a subarachnoid hemorrhage until a scan says otherwise. Tension headaches and sinus pain build gradually, and a migraine typically has a history of similar episodes.

quiz.q: Below what blood glucose value, with symptoms, is a patient considered hypoglycemic?
choices: 70 mg/dL
100 mg/dL
120 mg/dL
50 mg/dL
quiz.why: The working threshold is under 70 mg/dL with symptoms. 100 and 120 are within or above the normal fasting range, and waiting until 50 means letting a treatable patient deteriorate for no reason.

quiz.q: Fifteen minutes after one tube of oral glucose, a patient's repeat reading is 58 mg/dL and he is still confused but swallowing well. What should you do?
choices: Withhold further sugar and transport
Give a second dose of oral glucose and recheck again in 15 minutes
Give glucagon 1 mg intramuscularly
Give him a large meal to sustain the level
quiz.why: The rule of 15 repeats the dose until the glucose and symptoms improve, and he still meets every requirement for oral administration. Glucagon is for patients who cannot swallow, and solid food is slow and risks aspiration in a confused patient.

quiz.q: Which set of findings fits diabetic ketoacidosis rather than hypoglycemia?
choices: Cold clammy skin, normal breathing, rapid onset over minutes
Combativeness with a normal breath odor and a glucose of 45
Warm dry skin, deep rapid breathing, fruity breath, onset over days
Pale sweaty skin with shaking and hunger
quiz.why: DKA develops over hours to days with dehydration, Kussmaul respirations compensating for acidosis, and ketone breath. The other three choices describe the adrenaline-driven, minutes-long picture of hypoglycemia.

quiz.q: An 82-year-old nursing home patient with type 2 diabetes is profoundly confused and severely dehydrated. Glucose reads high on the meter. Her breathing is unlabored and her breath has no unusual odor. What is most likely?
choices: Diabetic ketoacidosis
Hypoglycemia
Simple dehydration from poor intake
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
quiz.why: HHS occurs in older type 2 patients with extremely high glucose, severe dehydration, and altered mentation but without significant ketosis, which is why there is no Kussmaul breathing and no fruity odor. DKA would produce both of those.

quiz.q: A patient with abdominal pain is lying completely still with knees drawn up and says any movement makes it worse. What does this suggest?
choices: Kidney stone
Peritoneal irritation from an acute abdomen
Anxiety
Muscular strain
quiz.why: Parietal pain from an inflamed peritoneum is sharp, localized, and worsened by motion, so these patients hold still. A kidney stone produces colicky pain that makes patients pace and writhe because no position helps.

quiz.q: A 58-year-old woman reports epigastric burning with nausea and sweating for 40 minutes. She thinks it is indigestion. What should you consider first?
choices: Gastritis and give an antacid
Pancreatitis and position her forward
Acute myocardial infarction, particularly an inferior wall MI
Bowel obstruction and withhold fluids
quiz.why: Inferior wall infarcts commonly present as epigastric pain with nausea and diaphoresis, and women, diabetics, and older adults frequently lack classic chest pain. Treating it as indigestion is how these infarcts get missed.

quiz.q: A 70-year-old has severe back pain, a systolic of 84, and a mass above the navel that you can feel pulsating. Your partner suggests palpating firmly to measure it. What is the correct response?
choices: Palpate carefully in all four quadrants to map the mass
Palpate only during exhalation to reduce the risk
Have the patient bear down so the mass is easier to feel
Do not palpate further; handle him gently and transport rapidly with early notification
quiz.why: Pressure on a leaking aneurysm can convert a contained leak into free rupture, and the field diagnosis changes nothing about your treatment. Every variation on more palpation carries the same risk, and bearing down raises intra-abdominal pressure.

quiz.q: Which set of findings makes up the classic opioid triad?
choices: Pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression, and decreased level of consciousness
Dilated pupils, tachycardia, and agitation
Fever, stiff neck, and headache
Bradycardia, hypertension, and irregular respirations
quiz.why: Miosis, slow or absent breathing, and depressed consciousness together are nearly diagnostic of opioid toxicity. Dilated pupils with agitation is the stimulant picture, and the last choice is Cushing's triad from rising intracranial pressure.

quiz.q: You give intranasal naloxone to an apneic overdose patient and nothing changes after 2 minutes. What is most appropriate?
choices: Give a second intranasal dose and wait another 5 minutes
Continue bag-valve-mask ventilation and give a repeat dose per protocol
Conclude it is not an opioid and stop ventilating
Perform a sternal rub and reassess
quiz.why: Ventilation is the treatment that keeps the patient alive while naloxone works, and fentanyl analogs commonly require repeat dosing. Waiting without bagging leaves the patient hypoxic, and a failure to respond quickly does not rule opioids out.

quiz.q: A patient took both alprazolam and vodka and is unresponsive with slow shallow breathing and normal-sized pupils. What is the correct treatment?
choices: Naloxone 4 mg intranasally
Activated charcoal 50 g
Airway management and assisted ventilation with high-flow oxygen
Oral glucose to raise his level of consciousness
quiz.why: Naloxone reverses opioids only and will do nothing for benzodiazepines or alcohol, which is why the pupils are normal. Charcoal requires an alert patient who can protect the airway, and glucose treats hypoglycemia rather than sedative overdose.

quiz.q: A 22-year-old who used cocaine an hour ago has crushing chest pain, heart rate 148, blood pressure 196/108, and a temperature of 39.4 C. What are the two most urgent concerns?
choices: Dehydration and hypoglycemia
Opioid co-ingestion and respiratory depression
Anxiety and hyperventilation
Hyperthermia and myocardial ischemia from coronary spasm
quiz.why: Cocaine causes coronary artery spasm and genuine infarction in young people, and stimulant hyperthermia causes organ damage and death. Respiratory depression is not the stimulant pattern, and calling a temperature of 39.4 with chest pain anxiety misses both killers.

quiz.q: What is the telephone number for Poison Control in the United States?
quiz.why: 1-800-222-1222 reaches Poison Control from anywhere in the country, free and around the clock. The third number is an animal poison line, and the last was the former suicide prevention line, now replaced by 988.

quiz.q: Which ingestion is an appropriate candidate for activated charcoal, assuming medical direction approves and the patient is alert?
choices: Drain cleaner swallowed 20 minutes ago
An overdose of acetaminophen tablets 30 minutes ago
Gasoline siphoned accidentally 15 minutes ago
An iron supplement bottle emptied an hour ago
quiz.why: Charcoal binds many drugs including acetaminophen within about an hour of ingestion. Caustics like drain cleaner, hydrocarbons like gasoline, and metals like iron are all contraindications because charcoal either does not bind them or makes the injury worse.

quiz.q: Two workers in a greenhouse are found vomiting, drooling heavily, with tearing eyes, constricted pupils, and wet-sounding lungs. What is the priority?
choices: Give activated charcoal to both patients
Give naloxone for the constricted pupils
Protect yourself, decontaminate by removing clothing, and suction and ventilate aggressively
Move them into the ambulance immediately without decontamination
quiz.why: This is an organophosphate cholinergic crisis, where patients drown in their own secretions and the residue on clothing will contaminate rescuers and the ambulance. Naloxone does nothing for this toxidrome despite the small pupils, and charcoal does not address the airway.

quiz.q: What two findings together define heat stroke?
choices: Heavy sweating and muscle cramps
Cool clammy skin and nausea
Dry skin and thirst
Core temperature over 104 F and altered mental status
quiz.why: Heat stroke is a core temperature above 104 F combined with altered mentation, and the skin may be dry in classic cases or soaked in exertional ones. Cramps and cool clammy skin with intact mentation describe heat cramps and heat exhaustion.

quiz.q: A hypothermic patient found in a cold garage is confused and has stopped shivering. What does the absence of shivering indicate?
choices: He has progressed to moderate hypothermia and can no longer generate heat
He is rewarming and improving
He never became hypothermic in the first place
He has a fever developing
quiz.why: Shivering ceases somewhere around 90 F as the body loses the ability to generate heat, so its absence in a cold confused patient marks worsening rather than recovery. This patient needs gentle handling and truncal rewarming.

quiz.q: A child is pulled from a pool in cardiac arrest after an unwitnessed submersion in cold water. What approach is correct?
choices: Withhold resuscitation because submersion arrests are not survivable
Begin ventilations early, start CPR, and continue resuscitation while rewarming
Perform abdominal thrusts first to clear water from the lungs
Restrict spinal motion before any airway management
quiz.why: Drowning arrest is caused by hypoxia, so ventilation comes early, and cold-water submersion justifies prolonged resuscitation under the not-dead-until-warm-and-dead principle. Abdominal thrusts delay ventilation and cause vomiting, and spinal restriction applies only when the mechanism suggests injury.

quiz.q: Which restraint practice is never acceptable?
choices: Restraining a patient supine with one provider per limb
Restraining a patient on their side with continuous airway monitoring
Restraining a patient in the prone position
Documenting the time restraints were applied and who was present
quiz.why: Prone restraint causes positional asphyxia and has killed patients, so it is never used regardless of how combative the patient is. Supine or side-lying restraint with adequate staffing, continuous monitoring, and documentation is the accepted practice.

quiz.q: A 68-year-old with a productive cough has a temperature of 38.6 C, heart rate 112, respiratory rate 24, and blood pressure 96/58, and is more confused than her baseline. What should you do?
choices: Transport routinely as a respiratory infection
Withhold notification until a blood pressure under 90 is documented
Treat only the confusion and request a psychiatric evaluation
Call a sepsis alert, support oxygenation, keep her warm, and notify the hospital early
quiz.why: She has a suspected infection plus fever, heart rate over 90, respiratory rate over 20, and altered mental status, which is well past the two-criteria threshold. Early notification is the intervention, because it moves antibiotics and fluids forward by critical minutes.

quiz.q: A dialysis patient missed two sessions and now has shortness of breath, crackles in both lungs, swollen legs, and generalized weakness. Beyond fluid overload, what should also concern you?
choices: Hyperkalemia, which can cause lethal cardiac rhythms
Hypoglycemia from missed meals
Dehydration from fluid restriction
Hypothermia from the dialysis circuit
quiz.why: Without dialysis, potassium accumulates and causes weakness and dangerous dysrhythmias, which is why missed sessions are a cardiac emergency and not just a breathing problem. Fluid overload is why he is wet, and dehydration is the opposite of his problem.

scenarios.title: Dispatched: allergic reaction at a restaurant
scenarios.intro:
It is 1920 on a Friday. Dispatch sends you to a busy Thai restaurant for a woman having an allergic reaction. A manager waves you toward a back table where a group of six is standing around one seated woman.

Her friend meets you at the door and says she ordered something she thought was safe and took two bites about ten minutes ago. She has a peanut allergy. Her purse is on the table and the friend says "I think she has one of those pens in there."

The closest ED is `9 minutes` away. ALS is available and about `6 minutes` out.

steps.prompt: She is `29`, sitting forward, flushed, with raised red welts across her chest and neck. She is scratching her arms, coughing between sentences, and says her throat feels "thick." She just vomited into a napkin. She can still speak in short sentences.

choices.text: Call it anaphylaxis now: skin, respiratory, and gastrointestinal involvement after a known allergen
choices.feedback: Correct. Two or more systems after a likely exposure is the definition, and she has three. Her blood pressure being 104 systolic does not change that, and waiting for it to fall is waiting too long.

choices.text: Call it a moderate allergic reaction and give oxygen while you watch her
choices.feedback: Hives alone would be an allergic reaction. Hives plus throat tightness plus vomiting is systemic, and the drug that treats it is not oxygen.

choices.text: Ask her to describe her symptoms in more detail before deciding
choices.feedback: You already have what you need, and every sentence she speaks is costing her air. History gathering continues while treatment starts, not instead of it.

choices.text: Get a full set of vitals and lung sounds first, then decide
choices.feedback: Reasonable instinct, and lung sounds will be useful. But the decision to give epinephrine is made on the pattern, not on the numbers, and you already have the pattern.

steps.prompt: Her friend finds an unexpired epinephrine auto-injector labeled `0.3 mg` in the purse. Her throat tightness is worsening and you can now hear a high-pitched sound when she breathes in. What do you do?

choices.text: Give the 0.3 mg auto-injector intramuscularly into the outer middle third of her thigh
choices.feedback: Correct. Stridor means the airway is swelling, and epinephrine is the only drug that reverses swelling, bronchospasm, and vasodilation at once. The thigh gives the fastest peak level, about 8 minutes, and it works through clothing.

choices.text: Give the auto-injector into the deltoid because her sleeve is already rolled up
choices.feedback: The drug is right and the route is right, but the deltoid absorbs more slowly than the vastus lateralis. The auto-injector goes through jeans without trouble, so convenience is not a reason to pick the arm.

choices.text: Give an antihistamine first and hold the epinephrine in case she worsens
choices.feedback: Diphenhydramine handles itching. It does nothing for laryngeal swelling or a falling blood pressure, and giving it instead of epinephrine appears in nearly every review of anaphylaxis deaths.

choices.text: Give albuterol by nebulizer for the airway sound and reassess in 5 minutes
choices.feedback: That sound is stridor from swelling in the upper airway, not a wheeze from the lower airway, and albuterol does not shrink swollen tissue. Albuterol has a role here, but only after the epinephrine.

steps.prompt: You give the epinephrine at `1927` into the left lateral thigh. She is now in the ambulance on oxygen. At `1932` the hives are slightly less angry but she is still stridorous, still coughing, and her pressure has dropped. She is becoming quieter.

choices.text: Lay her supine with the legs elevated and prepare a second dose of epinephrine per protocol
choices.feedback: Correct. This is distributive shock, and unlike trauma, leg elevation genuinely helps here. Epinephrine can be repeated at 5 to 15 minutes when symptoms persist, and a falling pressure with continued stridor is exactly that situation.

choices.text: Hold further epinephrine because her heart rate is already 138
choices.feedback: Tachycardia is the expected effect of the drug and of the shock itself. Withholding epinephrine from a hypotensive stridorous patient because of a fast pulse is how this call goes wrong.

choices.text: Sit her fully upright since she says it is easier to breathe that way
choices.feedback: Upright helps breathing but worsens brain perfusion at a systolic of 84. A compromise of semi-recumbent with the legs up is better, and the real answer is the second dose.

choices.text: Give albuterol and continue to the hospital without further epinephrine
choices.feedback: Albuterol is a reasonable adjunct for persistent bronchospasm but it does nothing for her blood pressure or for upper airway swelling. She needs the second epinephrine dose.

steps.prompt: You give a second dose of epinephrine at `1934`. Within four minutes her stridor resolves, the hives are fading, and she is talking normally. She says she feels much better and asks whether she really needs to go to the hospital, since she is supposed to fly out in the morning.

choices.text: Explain the biphasic risk and strongly encourage transport, documenting carefully if she still refuses
choices.feedback: Correct. Up to 20 percent of patients get a second wave, usually within 8 hours, while epinephrine lasts only 10 to 20 minutes. Naming that specific risk is what usually changes the answer.

choices.text: Accept the refusal since two doses of epinephrine have clearly worked
choices.feedback: The drug working is not the same as the reaction being over. Mast cells can release a second wave hours later, by which time she will be alone at home.

choices.text: Tell her she is legally required to be transported
choices.feedback: She is alert, oriented, and has the right to refuse. Threatening her destroys the only thing that will actually get her in the truck, which is trust.

choices.text: Have her take an antihistamine and follow up with her allergist tomorrow
choices.feedback: An antihistamine does not prevent a biphasic reaction, and tomorrow is well past the window in which the second wave usually happens.

steps.prompt: She agrees to go. On the `9`-minute ride she stays stable. What belongs in your radio report and your handoff?

choices.text: Allergen, time of exposure, systems involved, both epinephrine doses with times and site, and the response to each
choices.feedback: Correct. The two epinephrine times are what the ED uses to decide her observation period, and the systems involved justify the anaphylaxis diagnosis rather than an allergic reaction.

choices.text: Just say allergic reaction, treated with epinephrine, now stable
choices.feedback: Too thin. Without the times and the doses, the ED cannot judge how long she needs to be watched or whether she is already in a rebound.

choices.text: Report her current vital signs only, since she is now improved
choices.feedback: Her current numbers are the least informative part of this call. What matters clinically is how sick she was and what it took to reverse it.

choices.text: Report that she initially refused transport and changed her mind
choices.feedback: Worth documenting, but it is not the clinical information the receiving team needs to plan her observation and her discharge prescription.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern: **two systems, or hypotension after exposure, equals anaphylaxis**, and the answer is epinephrine intramuscularly in the lateral thigh. She had skin, respiratory, and gastrointestinal involvement before her pressure ever dropped, which was the moment to treat.

Watch what her vitals did after the first dose. The hives faded slightly but the systolic fell from `104` to `84` and the stridor persisted. Partial improvement is not improvement, and a second dose at `5–15 minutes` is expected, not exceptional. Tachycardia is never the reason to withhold it.

Stridor and wheeze are different problems. Stridor is upper airway swelling and needs epinephrine. Wheeze is lower airway constriction, where albuterol helps — after the epinephrine, never instead.

Finally, the refusal. Epinephrine lasts `10–20 minutes`; a biphasic reaction can arrive up to `8 hours` later. Naming that number is what moves patients.

scenarios.title: Dispatched: 74F, possible stroke
scenarios.intro:
You are dispatched at 0712 to a private residence for a woman who "can't talk right." Her daughter called from the kitchen and is waiting at the door.

Your system has three destination options: a community hospital `7 minutes` away with no stroke designation, a primary stroke center `15 minutes` away that gives thrombolytics, and a comprehensive stroke center `29 minutes` away that also performs thrombectomy.

steps.prompt: She is `74`, seated at the kitchen table, awake and looking frightened. Her words come out slurred and partly garbled. The right side of her mouth droops. Her daughter says she came downstairs like this about `15 minutes` ago. What is the first thing you do?

choices.text: Give aspirin, since most strokes are caused by clots
choices.feedback: No. You cannot tell an ischemic stroke from a hemorrhagic one in the field, and aspirin given into a brain bleed makes it worse. Aspirin is for chest pain, not stroke.

choices.text: Run a stroke scale and check a blood glucose
choices.feedback: Correct. The stroke scale confirms the pattern and the glucose rules out the one mimic that reverses in minutes. Both take under a minute and both change what happens next.

choices.text: Apply oxygen by non-rebreather at 15 lpm to protect the brain
choices.feedback: Her saturation is 97 percent. Oxygen above a normal saturation does not help stroke patients and may harm them. Oxygen is indicated only under 94 percent.

choices.text: Lower her blood pressure by having her lie flat and relax
choices.feedback: Do not chase a high blood pressure in a stroke. That pressure is often the body pushing blood past an obstruction, and dropping it can extend the injury.

steps.prompt: Glucose reads `112 mg/dL`. Run the scale. Her smile is asymmetric with the right side lagging. Asked to hold both arms out with eyes closed, her right arm drifts down within `6 seconds`. She cannot repeat "you can't teach an old dog new tricks" clearly. She also says the room is spinning and she sees double.

choices.text: Three abnormal Cincinnati findings plus balance and vision changes; this is a stroke and a BE-FAST positive
choices.feedback: Correct. Any one abnormal Cincinnati item is about a 72 percent probability; she has all three. The vertigo and double vision are the BE and the E, which point toward the posterior circulation.

choices.text: The dizziness and double vision suggest an inner ear problem rather than a stroke
choices.feedback: That is exactly the trap BE-FAST was created to close. Posterior circulation strokes present with balance and vision complaints and get written off as vertigo.

choices.text: Only the speech finding counts, since arm drift can be from arthritis
choices.feedback: Drift within 10 seconds in a patient with a matching facial droop is a neurologic finding, not a joint problem. Discounting items one at a time is how strokes get downgraded.

choices.text: It is a stroke, but the glucose of 112 means you should still consider a metabolic cause
choices.feedback: Keeping an open mind is fine, but 112 is a normal glucose and it has already done its job by excluding hypoglycemia. Move on to the clock and the destination.

steps.prompt: The daughter says she found her this way at `0655`. You need the last known well time. What do you ask?

choices.text: Record 0655 as the last known well, since that is when the symptoms were discovered
choices.feedback: That is the discovery time, not the last known well. Using it could wrongly place her inside a treatment window she is not eligible for, and thrombolytics carry real bleeding risk.

choices.text: Ask who last saw or spoke with her when she was completely normal, and at what time
choices.feedback: Correct. Last known well is the last moment anyone observed her at baseline. Also get a phone number for that witness, because the neurologist will need to call them.

choices.text: Ask the patient herself when the symptoms started
choices.feedback: Worth trying, and sometimes it works. But she is aphasic and may have anosognosia, so a stroke patient is rarely a reliable historian about her own onset.

choices.text: Record the last known well as unknown and let the hospital sort it out
choices.feedback: An unknown last known well can disqualify her from treatment. Two minutes of questions in the kitchen is far more valuable than anything else you will do on this call.

steps.prompt: The daughter says they spoke on the phone at `2230` last night and her mother was completely normal, laughing about a TV show. Nobody saw her after that. It is now `0720`.

choices.text: Last known well 2230, which is about 8 hours 50 minutes ago; outside the thrombolytic window but possibly inside the thrombectomy window
choices.feedback: Correct. Past 4.5 hours she cannot receive clot-busting drugs based on a plain last known well, but thrombectomy for a large-vessel occlusion can be considered out to 24 hours. That distinction drives the destination.

choices.text: Last known well 0655, so she is well inside the 4.5-hour window
choices.feedback: That is the discovery time again. The correct clock started at 2230 when she was last seen normal.

choices.text: Last known well 2230, so nothing can be done and she can go to the closest hospital
choices.feedback: Being outside the drug window is not the end of the options. Thrombectomy extends to 24 hours for selected large-vessel strokes, which is exactly why the destination still matters.

choices.text: Split the difference and call it about 0300
choices.feedback: Never invent a time. A neurologist will make a treatment decision with real bleeding risk based on the number you hand over.

steps.prompt: Choose a destination and get her packaged. She is asking for water because her mouth is dry.

choices.text: Comprehensive stroke center 29 minutes away, head elevated 30 degrees, nothing by mouth, early stroke alert with the 2230 last known well and the daughter's phone number
choices.feedback: Correct. She is outside the drug window but potentially a thrombectomy candidate, and only the comprehensive center can do that. Nothing by mouth because stroke impairs swallowing, and the early alert assembles the team before you arrive.

choices.text: Community hospital 7 minutes away, because speed matters most in stroke
choices.feedback: Speed to a hospital that cannot treat her is not speed. They would have to arrange a transfer, and that costs far more than the 22 extra minutes.

choices.text: Primary stroke center 15 minutes away, since it is the middle option
choices.feedback: A defensible choice and far better than the community hospital, but a primary center gives thrombolytics she is no longer eligible for. The intervention she may qualify for lives at the comprehensive center.

choices.text: Comprehensive stroke center, and give her small sips of water on the way
choices.feedback: Right destination, wrong detail. Stroke frequently impairs swallowing, and aspiration pneumonia is a leading cause of death afterward. Nothing by mouth, sips included.

steps.prompt: You are 5 minutes out. What goes in the stroke alert?

choices.text: Age, BE-FAST findings, last known well of 2230, glucose 112, current vitals, anticoagulant history, and a callback number for the daughter
choices.feedback: Correct. That packet lets the hospital page neurology, clear the scanner, and start the eligibility conversation before the doors open. The callback number is the part crews forget and neurologists need.

choices.text: Possible stroke, 74-year-old female, ETA 5 minutes
choices.feedback: Better than nothing, but it triggers no decision. Without the last known well and the deficits, the team cannot pre-plan anything.

choices.text: Full head-to-toe assessment findings in narrative order
choices.feedback: A radio report is a decision tool, not a chart. Bury the last known well inside a long narrative and it will be missed.

choices.text: Her blood pressure and the fact that you did not treat it
choices.feedback: The blood pressure belongs in the report, but leading with it suggests it is the problem. The clock and the deficits are what drive the stroke pathway.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern: **the stroke call is a clock, a glucose, and a destination**. Everything else you do on scene is secondary.

The glucose came first because hypoglycemia is the one mimic that reverses in minutes, and at `112` it was excluded in under a minute. Aspirin stayed in the bag because you cannot separate a clot from a bleed in a kitchen, and oxygen stayed off because her saturation was `97%`.

Last known well was the whole case. `0655` was when she was found; `2230` was when she was last seen normal. That difference moved her from inside the `4.5-hour` thrombolytic window to outside it, and made the `24-hour` thrombectomy window the relevant one — which changed the destination from a primary to a comprehensive stroke center.

Two small details carry weight. She got nothing by mouth, because swallowing fails early in stroke and aspiration pneumonia kills survivors. And you brought the daughter's phone number, because the person who can confirm the timeline is almost never the person riding with you.

scenarios.title: Dispatched: unresponsive male in a bathroom
scenarios.intro:
At 0245 you are sent to a second-floor apartment for an unresponsive man. The caller is a roommate who says he found him on the bathroom floor and that "he's been using again."

Police arrive with you. The bathroom is small, the patient is wedged between the toilet and the tub, and there is a used syringe on the edge of the sink. Your ALS unit is `8 minutes` out; the ED is `12 minutes` away.

steps.prompt: He is roughly `30`, cyanotic around the lips, and does not respond to his name or a trapezius pinch. His pupils are `1 mm` and do not react. His chest rises about `4` times a minute, shallow. There is a syringe on the sink and you have not yet moved him.

choices.text: Give 4 mg intranasal naloxone right where he lies
choices.feedback: Naloxone is coming, but not first. It takes 2 to 5 minutes to work and he is hypoxic right now. Bagging fixes the thing that is actually killing him, and you cannot manage an airway in a space this tight.

choices.text: Ask police to secure the syringe, move him to open floor, open the airway, and begin bag-valve-mask ventilation with high-flow oxygen
choices.feedback: Correct. Sharps safety, then space, then oxygen. Hypoxia is what stops the heart in opioid overdose, and a bag-valve-mask works in seconds while naloxone takes minutes.

choices.text: Apply a non-rebreather at 15 lpm and monitor his saturation
choices.feedback: A mask only delivers oxygen to someone moving air. At 4 breaths a minute he is not, so the oxygen sits in the mask while his carbon dioxide climbs.

choices.text: Begin chest compressions because his heart rate is 52
choices.feedback: He has a pulse. The bradycardia is his heart responding to hypoxia, and it will correct once he is oxygenated. Compressions on a perfusing patient delay the ventilation he needs.

steps.prompt: He is out in the hallway on the floor. You have an oral airway in and are bagging at `10` breaths per minute with an oxygen reservoir. After `90` seconds his color is improving and the saturation is climbing. He is still not breathing on his own.

choices.text: Continue bagging and give naloxone 4 mg intranasally now
choices.feedback: Correct. Oxygenate first, then reverse. Now that the hypoxia is corrected, naloxone restores his own respiratory drive, and you keep bagging while it takes effect over the next 2 to 5 minutes.

choices.text: Stop bagging now that the saturation is 92 percent and watch him
choices.feedback: The saturation is 92 because you are breathing for him. Stop and it falls right back. Ventilation continues until he is breathing adequately on his own.

choices.text: Continue bagging and wait for ALS to give naloxone intravenously
choices.feedback: Bagging is keeping him alive, so this is not harmful. But intranasal naloxone is within your scope and works in 2 to 5 minutes, and ALS is still 6 minutes out.

choices.text: Give naloxone and stop ventilating so you can see whether it worked
choices.feedback: Never stop ventilating to test the drug. Naloxone needs minutes, and his oxygen will fall the entire time you are waiting to see something.

steps.prompt: Three minutes after the naloxone he starts breathing on his own at about `14` a minute, opens his eyes, and begins to gag. He is confused, sweating, and starting to swing his arms. A moment later he vomits.

choices.text: Remove the oral airway, turn him on his side, suction, and give him verbal space while keeping hands clear
choices.feedback: Correct. Vomiting and agitation are expected precipitated withdrawal, and the only real danger in it is aspiration. Side position plus suction handles that, and standing clear of swinging arms handles you.

choices.text: Give a second dose of naloxone to fully wake him up
choices.feedback: You titrate naloxone to breathing, not to wakefulness. He is breathing at 14 with a saturation of 97, so more naloxone only deepens the withdrawal and the vomiting.

choices.text: Hold him down until he calms so he does not hurt himself
choices.feedback: Physical restraint of a withdrawing patient escalates the fight and puts a vomiting patient on his back. Space and calm talk work better and faster here.

choices.text: Leave the oral airway in place in case he becomes unresponsive again
choices.feedback: Understandable caution, but an awake gagging patient will not tolerate it and it will provoke more vomiting. Pull it, keep it at hand, and reassess.

steps.prompt: Ten minutes later he is oriented, embarrassed, and angry about being "narcanned." He says he feels fine, wants to go back upstairs, and refuses transport. Police say they have no reason to hold him.

choices.text: Accept the refusal since he is oriented and his vitals are normal
choices.feedback: His vitals are normal because of a drug that will wear off before the opioid does. Post-naloxone refusals are a recognized way people die an hour after the ambulance leaves.

choices.text: Explain that naloxone lasts 30 to 90 minutes and may wear off before the opioid does, and strongly encourage transport
choices.feedback: Correct. Naming the specific number is what changes minds. Fentanyl in particular outlasts naloxone, and re-sedation alone in an apartment is the exact scenario to prevent.

choices.text: Tell him he has no choice because he was unconscious ten minutes ago
choices.feedback: He is alert and oriented now, so he has decision-making capacity. Arguing about authority rather than risk ends the conversation you need to have.

choices.text: Have the roommate agree to watch him for two hours instead of transport
choices.feedback: Better than leaving him alone, and worth arranging if he absolutely will not go. But a roommate cannot ventilate him, and the plan still depends on someone noticing in time.

steps.prompt: He agrees to be transported. Twenty minutes into a slow ride through road construction, he becomes quiet and then hard to rouse. His breathing slows and his pupils constrict again.

choices.text: Resume bag-valve-mask ventilation and repeat naloxone per protocol
choices.feedback: Correct. This is re-sedation, exactly what you warned him about. The sequence does not change: ventilate first, then reverse, and notify the receiving hospital that he required a repeat dose.

choices.text: Give naloxone again and continue to the hospital without ventilating
choices.feedback: Same error as the first call, just later. Naloxone takes minutes and he is hypoxic at 88 percent now. Ventilation comes first every time.

choices.text: Assume he is simply asleep after a long night and let him rest
choices.feedback: Pinpoint pupils with a respiratory rate of 6 and a falling saturation is not sleep. That combination is the opioid triad returning.

choices.text: Apply a non-rebreather and increase your driving speed
choices.feedback: Oxygen by mask cannot help a patient breathing 6 times a minute, and driving faster does not treat him. He needs your hands on a bag.

steps.prompt: He responds again and is breathing adequately on arrival. What belongs in your handoff?

choices.text: Total naloxone dose and route, the times of each dose, the fact that he re-sedated 20 minutes after the first, and how long you ventilated
choices.feedback: Correct. Re-sedation en route is the single most important thing the ED needs to know, because it tells them he needs extended observation and possibly an infusion rather than a quick discharge.

choices.text: Opioid overdose, given naloxone, now awake
choices.feedback: Incomplete. Without the re-sedation history, the ED may treat him as a routine reversal and discharge him into the same problem.

choices.text: The syringe found on the sink and the roommate's statement about drug use
choices.feedback: Useful context, but it is not the clinical fact that changes his disposition. The repeat dose and the re-sedation are.

choices.text: His current vital signs only, since he is now stable
choices.feedback: His current numbers describe a patient who looks fine, which is exactly the impression that gets a re-sedating patient discharged too soon.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern: **ventilate first, then reverse**. Opioids kill by switching off the drive to breathe, and the death is a hypoxic one. A bag-valve-mask works in seconds; naloxone needs `2–5 minutes`. Giving the drug first and watching is the most common error on this call, and his bradycardia of `52` was hypoxia, not a rhythm problem — it corrected with oxygen alone.

Titrate to breathing, not to wakefulness. Once he was moving air at `14` a minute with a saturation of `97%`, more naloxone would only have bought more vomiting and more fighting. Expect the withdrawal, plan for the emesis, and keep your body out of the arc of an arm.

Re-sedation is the whole reason this patient gets transported. Naloxone lasts `30–90 minutes`, which is shorter than most opioids and far shorter than fentanyl analogs and methadone. He proved it twenty minutes into the ride.

That is also what makes the handoff matter. "Overdose, got naloxone, now awake" describes a discharge. "Required a repeat dose and re-sedated en route" describes an observation bed.
